Imagine you go to a restaurant. You don’t walk into the kitchen and cook your own food. Instead, you look at a menu and tell the waiter what you want. The waiter carries your order to the kitchen, then brings your meal back to you when it’s ready.

An API is like that waiter. It is a messenger that carries messages back and forth between two different computer programs.

Here is a real example. When you look at the weather on your phone, your phone does not know if it is raining. It sends a message—through an API—to the weather company that keeps track of temperatures and storms. The API asks, “Is it raining there right now?” Then it carries the answer back to your phone so the screen can show you a little rain cloud.

Another example: when you book a taxi on your phone, the driver needs to know where you are. Your phone uses an API to ask a map company for the address. The API brings that answer back so the driver knows where to pick you up.

So, an API is simply a helpful go-between. It lets different phone or computer programs talk to each other and share what they know, without you having to do all the work yourself.
